walk/node: Here is the node from before. It multiplies x by W, and its result, z, flows through the rest of the graph to f.
walk/dz: Walking back from f, backprop has reached this node: the gradient on z, d z, has arrived. Two, and minus one.
walk/W: From it, the node found the gradient on W: one slope per weight.
walk/x0: But x was made by an earlier node, and that node can take its step only once the gradient on x arrives.
walk/dx: So this node owes a second answer: partial f, partial x, one slope per entry of x.
walk/name: x is the node's input, so this is called its input gradient: d x, in code. Hand it back, and the walk goes on.
fork/one: Follow one entry of x: x one, which is four.
fork/rows: Row zero of W, dotted with x, makes z zero. There x one is multiplied by two, the weight in column one.
fork/row1: Row one makes z one, and there x one is multiplied by one, again from column one.
fork/fork: So as a graph, x one forks: one wire to a multiply on the way to z zero, and one on the way to z one.
fork/twice: It is a value used twice. Walking back, it collects a gradient from each wire, and those add up.
fork/p0: Each multiply swaps. From z zero, x one gets the weight, two, times z zero's gradient, two: four.
fork/p1: From z one, it gets the weight, one, times minus one: minus one.
fork/sum: Four and minus one add up to three. That is partial f, partial x one.
fork/own: And the four in x one itself appears nowhere: a multiply hands each input the other one's value.
cols/c1: x one used the two weights down column one of W, each times the gradient of its own row. That is column one, dotted with d z.
cols/c0: Each entry of x does the same with its own column. Column zero is one and three: one times two, plus three times minus one, is minus one.
cols/c2: And column two gives minus four.
cols/T: Transposing W lays its columns down as rows: W transpose, three by two.
cols/Tdz: So the whole gradient is one product, W transpose, d z: each row of W transpose, dotted with d z.
cols/row: On the page, d z is written across, so the shapes can look like three by two, times one by two. Those do not fit.
cols/stand: But a vector multiplied by a matrix stands as a column, just as x does in W x. Stood up, d z is two by one.
cols/fit: Three by two, times two by one: the inner twos match, and out comes three by one. That is the shape of x, as its gradient must be.
try/aid: Shapes check the answer. d z, x transpose is two by three, like W: that is the gradient on W.
try/aid2: W transpose, d z has three entries, like x. And W times d z does not even fit: rows of three, against two numbers.
try/p1: Try one. W's first row is one, four, its second is two, minus three, and d z is three, minus one. What is partial f, partial x?
try/a1: Entry one meets column one of W: four and minus three. Dot it with d z: four times three, plus minus three times minus one. Twelve plus three is fifteen.
try/a2: Column zero is one and two: one times three, plus two times minus one, is one. With column one's fifteen, partial f, partial x is one, fifteen.
